title: Ancient Mystery Cults and Eleusis
description: Initiation, secrecy, and the most famous rite of the Greek world

concepts.title: What "Mysteries" Meant
concepts.contentHtml:
The Greek word mystērion comes from the verb myein, "to close", used of the eyes or the lips. You probably think of a mystery as a puzzle, but that sense came much later. A mystēs (plural mystai) was a person who had gone through a teletē, a rite of initiation, and was bound not to speak of what had been done or shown.

Walter Burkert's influential definition (Ancient Mystery Cults, 1987) calls the mysteries initiation rituals of a voluntary, personal and secret character that aimed at a change of mind through experience of the sacred. Civic religion was what a city did together, by birth and by duty: sacrifices, festivals, oaths. Mysteries were chosen. A candidate paid fees, fasted, was purified, and passed through a sequence of acts that most neighbors had never seen.

Burkert also stressed that the mysteries didn't compete as rival churches or demand exclusive membership. An Athenian initiated at Eleusis still sacrificed to Athena, and a Roman could be initiated into the rites of Isis and of Mithras both. What initiation offered, according to the texts that praise it, was a closer relationship with particular gods and, often, a better hope for what came after death.

Secrecy shapes the evidence. Most initiates kept their oath, so what survives comes from three kinds of source: the archaeology of sanctuaries, allusive praise by insiders, and later, hostile descriptions by Christian writers who wanted to expose the rites, each with its own distortions.

concepts.title: Eleusis: Demeter, Kore and the Sacred Way
concepts.contentHtml:
About 20 km west of Athens, at Eleusis, the Greek world held its most prestigious mysteries, in honor of Demeter and her daughter Kore ("the Maiden"), also called Persephone. The founding myth survives in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, probably composed in the 7th or 6th century BCE. Hades seizes Kore. Demeter searches for her, comes to Eleusis disguised as an old woman, and withholds the growth of grain until the gods agree to a compromise. Kore will spend part of each year below the earth and part above. The Hymn ends by calling blessed whoever has seen the rites Demeter taught there.

By the classical period the Greater Mysteries took place each autumn, in the month Boedromion (roughly September to October). Candidates walked in procession along the Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis. The climax came at night inside the Telesterion, a great roofed hall that could hold a few thousand people. Two Eleusinian families ran the rites. The hierophant ("revealer of sacred things") came from the Eumolpidai, and the torchbearer from the Kerykes. Initiation was unusually open. Men and women, free and enslaved, Greeks and Greek-speaking foreigners could take part, provided they weren't polluted by bloodshed. A returning initiate could become an epoptēs, a "viewer", in a higher stage.

Secrecy was enforced by law. In 415 BCE Alcibiades and others were accused of mocking the Mysteries in private houses, and the scandal helped drive him into exile. Later initiates included the emperors Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius, and Cicero, who wrote that Athens had given the world nothing better, since initiates learned how to live with joy and to die with better hope.

concepts.title: What We Know, What We Guess
concepts.contentHtml:
Ancient writers agree that things were shown, done and said at Eleusis, but the details are mostly guesswork. The Hymn tells how Demeter broke her fast with kykeon, a drink of barley, water and pennyroyal, and initiates drank it too. Clement of Alexandria, a Christian writer around 200 CE, quotes what he calls the Eleusinian password: "I fasted, I drank the kykeon, I took from the chest, having done my work I put it in the basket, and from the basket into the chest." Hippolytus of Rome claims the hierophant showed an ear of grain reaped in silence. Both are hostile witnesses with reasons to make the rites look trivial, and no insider account survives to check them.

In The Road to Eleusis (1978), R. Gordon Wasson, Albert Hofmann (the chemist who first synthesized LSD) and Carl Ruck proposed that the kykeon contained ergot, a fungus of grain whose alkaloids are chemically related to LSD. It remains speculative. No ancient source mentions a drug, ergot is a dangerous poison, and no residue from the Telesterion has confirmed it. Most specialists treat it as unproven.

The written evidence covers about a thousand years, from the Hymn to the end of the 4th century CE. Michael Cosmopoulos has argued from excavation that cult at Eleusis began in the Late Bronze Age, which would stretch the tradition toward 1,500 years or more; others doubt continuity across the Mycenaean collapse. The end is clearer. Theodosius I banned pagan sacrifice in 391 to 392 CE, and Alaric's Visigoths ravaged Eleusis around 395 to 396. The pagan writer Eunapius recorded that the last hierophant was an outsider from Thespiai who held the rank of "Father" in the rites of Mithras.

title: Dionysus, Orpheus and Isis
description: Bacchic rites, instructions for the dead, and an Egyptian goddess in Rome

concepts.title: Bacchic Rites and the Scandal of 186 BCE
concepts.contentHtml:
Dionysus, Bacchus to the Romans, was honored in public festivals, but he also had private rites conducted by voluntary groups called thiasoi. Euripides' Bacchae, first staged in 405 BCE, shows the god's women followers, the maenads, roaming the mountains in ecstasy. It is a tragedy, not a ritual manual, but it shows how Greeks imagined Bacchic frenzy.

Bacchic groups spread through Italy in the early 2nd century BCE, and in 186 BCE the Roman Senate moved against them. Livy, writing about 170 years later, gives this account. A young man, Publius Aebutius, is to be initiated by his mother and stepfather; his lover, the freedwoman Hispala Faecenia, warns him that the rites involve debauchery and murder; and the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus brings the matter to the Senate. Livy claims more than 7,000 men and women were implicated and many executed. His account is shaped by moral alarm and literary craft.

The decree itself survives. A bronze tablet found at Tiriolo in Calabria in 1640 records the Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus. It did not ban Bacchic worship outright. No man was to be a priest and no one a master of the group; common funds and mutual oaths were forbidden; and gatherings were limited to five people, no more than two men and three women, unless the urban praetor and the Senate gave permission. Historians read it as an effort to break up organized networks that the Senate could not control. The contemporary inscription and the later narrative tell somewhat different stories.

concepts.title: The Orphic Gold Tablets
concepts.contentHtml:
Orpheus, the legendary singer, was credited with poems on the origins of the gods and with rites of purification. Plato complains of wandering priests who sold purifications from books ascribed to Orpheus. What "Orphism" was is debated. Some scholars see a movement with shared doctrine; others, notably Radcliffe Edmonds, see a loose label applied to many authors and practitioners. The myth often cited as Orphic doctrine, in which the Titans tear apart the infant Dionysus and humans arise from their ashes, survives mostly in late sources, and Edmonds argues that its framing as an ancient doctrine of original sin is largely a modern construction.

The gold tablets offer direct evidence. These thin inscribed sheets of gold, placed with the dead, have been found in graves in southern Italy (Hipponion, Thurii, Petelia), Thessaly, Crete and elsewhere, dating from about 400 BCE into the Roman imperial period. Several give the soul directions: avoid the first spring, beside a white cypress, and go on to the lake of Memory, where guards stand. There the dead person should say, "I am a child of Earth and starry Sky," and ask for cold water to drink. Two ivy-leaf tablets from Pelinna in Thessaly, usually dated to the late 4th century BCE, tell the dead: "Tell Persephone that Bacchios himself released you."

Fritz Graf and Sarah Iles Johnston read the tablets as ritual texts for initiates who expected a privileged afterlife through Persephone and Dionysus. Related evidence comes from the Derveni papyrus, a charred roll found in 1962 near Thessaloniki and buried around 340 BCE, which contains a commentary on an Orphic poem about the gods' origins. It is often called the oldest surviving manuscript in Europe.

concepts.title: Isis in the Roman World and the Golden Ass
concepts.contentHtml:
Isis was an ancient Egyptian goddess, wife of Osiris and mother of Horus. Under the Ptolemies her cult was recast for Greek speakers alongside Serapis, a god promoted at Alexandria, and spread through ports and trade networks across the Mediterranean. Greek inscriptions called aretalogies have Isis list her powers in the first person: she separated earth from sky, gave laws, and rules the sea.

Rome's relationship with her was uneasy. In the 50s and 40s BCE the Senate repeatedly ordered her shrines in the city pulled down. Josephus tells a scandalous story of Tiberius destroying her temple in 19 CE, which some scholars suspect is largely literary. Yet the cult persisted and later won imperial favor. The Iseum Campense in the Campus Martius became a major temple, and the temple of Isis at Pompeii, rebuilt after an earthquake in 62 CE, was buried by Vesuvius in 79.

The fullest description of an initiation from any ancient mystery comes from fiction. In Book 11 of Apuleius's Metamorphoses, known as The Golden Ass (2nd century CE), Lucius, turned into a donkey by magic, regains human form by eating roses carried in an Isis procession at Cenchreae near Corinth. After fasting and purification he is initiated, and he tells the reader only this much: he approached the boundary of death, was carried through all the elements, saw the sun shining at midnight, and stood face to face with the gods above and below. Then he refuses to say more. At one point the text calls Lucius "a man of Madauros", Apuleius's own hometown, so some readers think the scene draws on the author's experience.

title: Mithras
description: Cave temples, a bull-slaying god, and a long debate about Persian roots

concepts.title: Mithraea and the Tauroctony
concepts.contentHtml:
The Roman cult of Mithras is first clearly attested in the late 1st century CE and flourished until the late 4th. It is known mostly from archaeology. Members met in a mithraeum, a long, narrow room built to imitate a cave, often underground or windowless, with raised benches along both sides where perhaps 20 to 40 men reclined for ritual meals. Remains survive from Hadrian's Wall to Dura-Europos on the Euphrates, with dense clusters along the Rhine and Danube frontiers, at Rome, and at its port Ostia, where more than a dozen have been found. Members were soldiers, imperial slaves and freedmen, officials and merchants. There is no secure evidence of women members.

At the end of every mithraeum stood the cult image, the tauroctony. Mithras, in a Phrygian cap, kneels on a bull and drives a knife into its neck, usually looking back over his shoulder. A dog and a snake reach for the blood, a scorpion attacks the bull's genitals, a raven watches, and ears of grain often sprout from the tail. The Sun and Moon look on from the upper corners, and two torchbearers flank the scene: Cautes with torch raised, Cautopates with torch lowered. Other images show Mithras born from a rock and feasting with the Sun on the bull's hide.

There is no Mithraic scripture and almost no insider writing. Meaning has to be inferred from images, from inscriptions such as the painted verses in the mithraeum under Santa Prisca in Rome, and from remarks by outsiders, including Christian critics. Interpretations of the cult vary widely.

concepts.title: Seven Grades of Initiation
concepts.contentHtml:
Mithraists were ranked in grades. Jerome, writing around 400 CE, lists seven, and a mosaic floor in the Mithraeum of Felicissimus at Ostia shows their symbols in sequence, each paired with a planet: Corax (Raven, Mercury), Nymphus (Bridegroom, Venus), Miles (Soldier, Mars), Leo (Lion, Jupiter), Perses (Persian, Moon), Heliodromus (Sun-runner, Sun) and Pater (Father, Saturn). The Father led the community, and 4th-century inscriptions from Rome even name a "Father of Fathers".

Initiation involved ordeals and symbolic acts. Tertullian, a Christian writer around 200 CE, says a Soldier was offered a crown on a sword and had to refuse it, declaring that Mithras was his crown, and that Mithras marked his soldiers on the forehead. Wall paintings in the mithraeum at Santa Maria Capua Vetere show a blindfolded, naked initiate kneeling before figures who stand over him. The philosopher Porphyry, in the 3rd century, reports that Lions had honey poured on their hands instead of water, because honey cleanses and is akin to fire.

How the grades worked in practice is debated. Some scholars think every member climbed through all seven; others suspect the full ladder was an ideal, with many members holding a low grade or no recorded grade at all. The planetary order fits an idea the 2nd-century critic Celsus attributes to the Mithraists, preserved in Origen's reply to him: a ladder with seven gates, symbolizing the soul's passage through the planetary spheres.

concepts.title: Persian Roots and the Jesus Comparisons
concepts.contentHtml:
Mithra is a genuine Indo-Iranian god. He appears in a treaty between the Hittites and the kingdom of Mitanni in the 14th century BCE, and in the Avestan hymn to Mithra as a god of contracts and light. The Romans dressed Mithras as a Persian. In volumes published in the 1890s, Franz Cumont argued that the Roman mysteries were essentially Persian religion carried west, and his view dominated for decades.

At the First International Congress of Mithraic Studies in Manchester in 1971, scholars including John Hinnells and Richard Gordon attacked the Cumont model. Iranian sources never show Mithra killing a bull (in Zoroastrian texts the primordial bull is killed by the evil spirit Ahriman), and the grades and cave temples have no Iranian parallels. David Ulansey (1989) proposed that the tauroctony is a star map, its figures matching constellations linked to an age when the spring equinox lay in Taurus. Most specialists now see a Roman-era creation that borrowed Persian prestige and names; how much Iranian content it carried is still argued.

Popular claims that the Jesus story copied Mithras (virgin birth on 25 December, twelve disciples, death and resurrection) fail on the evidence. Mithras was born from a rock; no source gives him disciples, a death or a resurrection; and 25 December appears in a Roman calendar of 354 CE as the birthday of Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, not as a Mithraic feast. The Roman cult is first attested after Christianity began, so gospel borrowing is implausible. The reverse claim also fails: Justin Martyr's charge, around 150 CE, that demons imitated the Eucharist in Mithraic bread-and-water rites is polemic.

title: Gnostics and Manichaeans
description: Salvation through knowledge, and Mani's religion of Light from Carthage to China

concepts.title: Gnosis and the Trouble with a Category
concepts.contentHtml:
"Gnosticism" traditionally names a range of 2nd- and 3rd-century movements, among them the Valentinians and the so-called Sethians, who taught that salvation comes through gnōsis, knowledge of the soul's divine origin, and that the material world was made by a lesser creator, the demiurge. Until the 20th century these groups were known mainly through opponents such as Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around 180 CE. The Nag Hammadi codices, found in Egypt in 1945 and covered in the Western Esotericism topic, let many of them speak in their own words.

Many of these movements were initiatory in a real sense. Valentinian Christians, by their opponents' account, sorted humanity into spiritual, soul-bearing and material people, and reserved their deepest teaching for those judged spiritual. Several texts present themselves as secret words given to a chosen disciple, and rites such as the "bridal chamber" appear in texts like the Gospel of Philip.

The label itself is now contested. Michael Williams (Rethinking "Gnosticism", 1996) and Karen King (What Is Gnosticism?, 2003) argued that the category lumps together groups that did not call themselves Gnostics and did not share one system; it was assembled largely from heresy-hunters' lists. Williams proposed speaking instead of "biblical demiurgical" traditions. Other scholars keep "Gnostic" for a narrower set of texts. Mani's movement, which drew on this world of ideas, was different: a missionary church with a founder, an organized hierarchy and its own written scripture.

concepts.title: Mani and the Religion of Light
concepts.contentHtml:
Mani was born in 216 CE in Babylonia, then under Parthian rule and soon part of the Sasanian Persian empire. The Cologne Mani Codex, a tiny Greek parchment book of the 4th or 5th century, first published in 1970, shows that he grew up in a Jewish-Christian baptist community that looked to the prophet Elchasai and purified its members and food with water. Mani reported revelations from a heavenly "Twin", broke with the sect around 240, and began to preach, traveling as far as the Indus region.

The Sasanian king Shapur I received him, and Mani wrote a book in Middle Persian, the Shabuhragan, for him. Unusually for a founder, Mani wrote his own scriptures, to prevent the distortions he believed had befallen Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus, whom he counted as forerunners; he called himself an apostle of Jesus Christ. Under Bahram I, at the urging of the Zoroastrian priest Kerdir, Mani was imprisoned at Gundeshapur and died in captivity, in 274 or 277 by the main rival datings.

Mani taught two eternal principles, Light and Darkness, and three times: a past when they were separate, a present of mixture, and a future of final separation. Particles of Light are trapped in matter, including plants and human bodies. The church had two classes. The Elect lived strict lives: celibate, vegetarian, without property, and forbidden to harvest or cook, since that would injure the Light. The Hearers, the laity, married, worked and brought food to the Elect, whose bodies were believed to release the Light it contained. The sun and moon were ships carrying freed Light home.

concepts.title: From Carthage to Quanzhou
concepts.contentHtml:
Manichaeism spread fast. By the late 3rd century it had reached Egypt and North Africa, and around 300 CE Diocletian ordered its leaders burned as followers of a Persian creed. Coptic Manichaean books found at Medinet Madi in 1929 and letters excavated at Kellis in Egypt's Dakhla Oasis show communities at prayer and at work.

Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer for about nine years, from his late teens to his late twenties, drawn by a clean answer to the problem of evil: evil came from an independent Darkness, not from God. He grew disillusioned when the Manichaean bishop Faustus, visiting Carthage around 383, could not answer his questions about astronomy. After his conversion Augustine wrote against the Manichaeans for decades, and much of what the Latin West knew of them came through him.

Eastward, Sogdian merchants carried the faith along the Silk Roads. A Manichaean teacher presented scripture at the Tang court in 694, and an edict of 732 allowed only foreigners to practice it. In about 762 the Uyghur ruler Bögü Qaghan adopted it as the religion of his state. After the Uyghur empire fell, the Tang suppressed it in the 840s, but it survived in southeastern China as the "Religion of Light", blending with Buddhist and Daoist forms. At Cao'an near Quanzhou in Fujian, a rock-cut statue of Mani as the "Buddha of Light", donated according to its inscription in 1339, still stands. The founding Ming emperor reportedly moved against the religion, yet manuscripts first reported in Xiapu county in 2008 show Manichaean hymns still used by local ritual masters.

title: Living Esoteric Faiths of the Middle East
description: Mandaeans, Yazidis, Druze and Alawites: closed communities that survived

concepts.title: The Mandaeans
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mandaeans are a small ethno-religious community whose traditional home is the river country of southern Iraq and Iran's Khuzestan province. Their name comes from manda, "knowledge", in Mandaic, their own dialect of Aramaic. Their cosmology is dualistic: a world of Light, ruled by the Great Life, stands against a world of darkness, and the soul, trapped in the body, rises back to the Light after death if properly prepared.

Ritual centers on water. Masbuta, baptism by full immersion in flowing, "living" water, is repeated throughout life, traditionally on Sundays, rather than performed once. Any river used for baptism is called yardna, "Jordan". Mandaeans honor John the Baptist as a great teacher, though not as their founder, while their texts treat Jesus and Moses negatively. Their chief scripture, the Ginza Rabba ("Great Treasure"), has a Right part on cosmology, history and morals and a Left part on the soul's ascent. Other books include the Book of John and the Qolasta, a collection of prayers.

Origins are debated. Some scholars accept the community's own tradition of a western origin near the Jordan valley in the early centuries CE; others are skeptical. Jorunn Buckley's study of manuscript colophons, the scribes' notes listing earlier copyists, traces named copyists back to the 3rd century CE. The modern story is one of flight. Iraq had perhaps 60,000 to 75,000 Mandaeans before 2003; most have since left after kidnappings and killings, and the largest communities now live in Australia, Sweden and the United States, where finding suitable rivers and trained priests is a practical problem.

concepts.title: The Yazidis
concepts.contentHtml:
The Yazidis are a Kurmanji-speaking religious community whose homeland is northern Iraq, especially the Sinjar mountains and the Sheikhan district around their holiest shrine at Lalish, with communities in Syria, Turkey, Armenia and Georgia and a large diaspora in Germany. Their tradition holds that one God entrusted the world to seven holy beings, chief among them Tawûsê Melek, the Peacock Angel. Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir, a 12th-century Sufi who settled at Lalish and is buried there, became a central holy figure. The religion draws on Iranian, Sufi and local traditions, and how these combined is debated.

Religious knowledge is mainly oral. Hymns called qewl, sung by trained reciters (qewwal), carry theology and sacred history. Two "sacred books" published in the early 20th century, the Black Book and the Book of Revelation, are widely regarded by scholars as forgeries produced for outside buyers, even if they echo genuine tradition. Society is divided into hereditary groups (sheikhs, pirs and murids) with rules on marriage. One is born Yazidi; conversion into the faith is not possible.

Neighbors long identified Tawûsê Melek with Satan, an equation Yazidis reject, and the slander of "devil worship" was used to justify repeated massacres under Ottoman and local rulers. In August 2014 the Islamic State (ISIS) overran Sinjar, killing men and older women, forcing conversions, and enslaving thousands of women and children. A household survey published in 2017 estimated about 3,100 killed and 6,800 kidnapped in a few days. In 2016 a United Nations commission of inquiry concluded that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis. Nadia Murad, a survivor, shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize.

concepts.title: The Druze and the Alawites
concepts.contentHtml:
The Druze faith emerged in Fatimid Egypt in the early 11th century around the caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah (r. 996 to 1021), whom believers regard as a manifestation of the divine unity, and the preacher Hamza ibn Ali. Adherents call themselves al-Muwahhidun, "the unitarians"; the name Druze comes from al-Darazi, an early preacher they regard as a heretic. The "call" to the faith opened in 1017 and was closed in about 1043 (some sources give 1042). Since then no converts have been admitted, and Druze identity passes by birth. Scripture is the Epistles of Wisdom, and teaching includes immediate rebirth of souls in new human bodies.

Within the community the uqqal ("the knowing") are initiated into the texts and inner teachings after a period of testing, wear distinctive dress, and meet in prayer houses; women as well as men can be initiated. The majority, the juhhal ("the uninstructed"), are not taught the scriptures. Roughly a million Druze live in Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Jordan.

The Alawites, historically called Nusayris after Muhammad ibn Nusayr, a 9th-century follower of the eleventh Shi'i imam, live mainly in Syria's coastal mountains, with communities in Turkey and Lebanon. Their doctrine, systematized by al-Khasibi in the 10th century, venerates a divine triad associated with Ali, Muhammad and Salman al-Farisi, and is taught secretly to initiated men. The 14th-century jurist Ibn Taymiyya condemned them as unbelievers. The name Alawi came into general use under the French Mandate. Hafez al-Assad, an Alawite, took power in 1970; after the Assad government fell in December 2024, Alawite civilians suffered reprisal killings, notably in March 2025.

title: Why Faiths Keep Secrets
description: Hidden liturgy, hidden Christians, small survivors, and how scholars study silence

concepts.title: The Disciplina Arcani
concepts.contentHtml:
Early Christians were not always secretive. Around 155 CE Justin Martyr described baptism and the Eucharist in plain detail in an open appeal to the emperor Antoninus Pius, precisely to show that the rites were harmless. By the 4th century, as large numbers sought baptism, many churches treated the core rites differently. Catechumens, those preparing for baptism, were dismissed before the Eucharist. The Creed and the Lord's Prayer were "handed over" to candidates orally shortly before baptism and recited back from memory, and the meaning of the sacraments was explained only afterward, during Easter week.

The clearest witness is Cyril of Jerusalem, bishop from about 350. His lectures to candidates tell them not to repeat what they hear to catechumens or outsiders. A separate set of Mystagogical Catecheses, explaining baptism, anointing and the Eucharist to the newly baptized, is attributed to him or to his successor John. Ambrose of Milan taught in a similar way. The label disciplina arcani, "discipline of the secret", is not ancient. It was coined in the 17th century during Catholic and Protestant controversy, when both sides used the practice to explain why some doctrines were not stated openly in early texts.

Scholars offer several reasons for the reserve, not mutually exclusive: reverence for the rites, protection from mockery, the teaching power of withholding and then revealing, and the prestige of the language of the pagan mysteries, which Christian writers borrowed even while condemning the cults themselves. The practice faded once nearly everyone was baptized in infancy.

concepts.title: Japan's Hidden Christians
concepts.contentHtml:
Jesuit missionaries led by Francis Xavier reached Japan in 1549, and by about 1600 there may have been some 300,000 Christians, concentrated in Kyushu. Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered missionaries expelled in 1587, and 26 Christians were crucified at Nagasaki in 1597. In 1614 the Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity outright. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 to 1638, households had to register with Buddhist temples, and in the Nagasaki area people were made to tread on Christian images (fumi-e) to prove they were not believers.

Mancio Konishi, usually described as the last Catholic priest in the country, was killed in 1644. Villages around Nagasaki, in Sotome, Urakami, the Goto islands, Hirado and Ikitsuki, then kept the faith on their own. Lay leaders baptized infants and kept the church calendar. Prayers called orasho (from Latin oratio) were memorized and passed down in a mix of Latin, Portuguese and Japanese whose meaning was partly lost. Statues of the Buddhist bodhisattva Kannon could serve as concealed images of Mary.

On 17 March 1865, villagers from Urakami approached the French priest Bernard Petitjean at the new Oura church in Nagasaki and revealed that Christians had survived about 250 years since the 1614 ban. A final persecution followed before the ban was lifted in 1873. Many then rejoined the Catholic Church, but some communities kept their ancestors' practice separately; these are the Kakure Kirishitan in the strict sense. Their numbers fell to an estimated 1,000 to 1,500 by 1999 and are now a few hundred at most. UNESCO listed hidden Christian sites in the Nagasaki region as World Heritage in 2018.

concepts.title: Small Survivors and Studying Silence
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every closed community is secretive. The Samaritans trace their descent to the northern Israelite tribes and hold that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, is the place God chose. Their Torah, the Samaritan Pentateuch, is written in a script descended from paleo-Hebrew. The Judean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple on Gerizim in the late 2nd century BCE, yet Samaritans still sacrifice lambs there at Passover. They numbered fewer than 200 in the early 20th century and about 900 today, in Kiryat Luza on Gerizim and in Holon near Tel Aviv.

Scholars studying what insiders will not tell use several routes, each flawed: hostile outsiders (Christian attacks on the mysteries, Muslim heresy-writers on the Druze and Alawites); material remains such as mithraea and gold tablets; texts that escaped, like the Druze manuscripts that reached European libraries and that Silvestre de Sacy analyzed in 1838; testimony from former members; and fieldwork with insiders who decide what to share. The linguist Kenneth Pike's terms emic (an insider's categories) and etic (an outsider's), from 1954, help keep these perspectives apart.

There is also an ethical problem. For the Druze, Yazidis and Alawites, secrecy partly protected small communities from hostile majorities, and publishing what they guard can cause harm. Georg Simmel's 1906 essay on secrecy argued that secrets create bonds and boundaries whatever their content. Hugh Urban (1998) urged scholars to study what secrecy does and who controls it, rather than only trying to expose what is hidden.
